name: Pál-völgyi Cave
description: A cave in the Buda hills found in 1904 and shown to visitors since 1919. Warm water rising through limestone dissolved its passages, and a guided route of about 500 metres passes dripstones, calcite crystals and sharp changes of level in a system that sources put at 12 km or more.

children.text: The Pál-völgyi Cave lies in the Buda hills at Szépvölgyi út 162. Its own site says it was found in 1904 and has been open to the public since 1919. The commonly told account of the discovery is that the ground collapsed under a grazing sheep in a quarry in July 1904 (some accounts say a goat), and that János Bagyura, the quarry owner's son, went in after it and found the cave; Telex says Bagyura then led the exploration.

The cave is a karst cave shaped by water from below. Telex reports that carbonic-acid-rich thermal water rising through fractured limestone dissolved the passages, and that rainwater later widened them once the cave stood further above the level of the Danube. Showcaves.com adds that the same process is linked to the thermal springs Budapest is known for. About eight of the 41 algae species found there date from the time when thermal water flooded the cave, and around 660 bats hibernate in it each winter.

Length figures depend on the source and the year. Showcaves.com gives about one kilometre in 1910, about four in 1980 and 12 mapped by 1998, while Telex says the cave and the nearby caves it was linked with after 2000, including the Mátyás-hegy and Harcsaszájú caves, form a system of 31 kilometres, which it calls Hungary's longest. Only about 500 metres are open to the public.

On the guided route you pass unique dripstones, glittering calcite crystals, narrow passages and dramatic level changes. Showcaves.com names areas such as the Theatre Hall, about 12 metres high, a Long Passage where ultraviolet light makes the calcite glow, and Fairyland, the most heavily decorated part. The cave was used as an air-raid shelter between 1939 and 1944. Telex adds that the former mine guardhouse was converted into a visitor centre in 2022.
Good to know
The cave's own page says to take bus 65 from Kolosy tér toward Szépvölgyi dűlő and get off at the Pál-völgyi cseppkőbarlang stop.
The route has over 400 stairs and one ladder, is not accessible for people with limited mobility, and is not suitable for children under 5 or under 115 cm tall.
The constant temperature is about 11 degrees Celsius, so bring a sweater even in summer; dogs are not allowed.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and tour languages before you go.

historyIntro: Pál-völgyi Cave reveals another Budapest beneath the streets: a landscape of limestone passages, unusual shapes and long geological timescales.

historySections.heading: A natural world under the Buda Hills

children.text: The cave belongs to the limestone and thermal-water landscape of the Buda Hills. Passageways and mineral formations reveal the action of water over very long periods, far removed from the familiar streets and monumental buildings above.

historySections.heading: From discovery to protected visitor route

children.text: Selected parts have become an interpreted natural attraction, with guided access designed to protect the cave environment. The marked visitor route is not the same as unrestricted access to the wider underground system.

name: Budapest Zoo & Botanical Garden
description: Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden in City Park opened on 9 August 1866 and is one of the oldest zoos in the world. Its main gate, Elephant House and Palm House date from the 1909-1912 reconstruction, when Art Nouveau buildings were added, and it was rebuilt after the Second World War.

children.text: Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden lies within City Park (Városliget) and covers about 18.4 hectares. It opened to the public on 9 August 1866 and is described as the oldest zoo in Hungary and one of the oldest in the world. According to the zoo's own history, a private company set up by four founders established it; the best known of them is János Xántus, who later became director.

Most of the surviving historic buildings date from a major renovation between 1909 and 1912, during which the zoo was closed; it reopened on 20 May 1912. After the operating company went bankrupt in 1907, the City Council took over. The zoo's history credits Károly Kós, Dezső Zrumeczky, Kornél Neuschloss and Gyula Végh with designing most of the buildings from this period, including the main gate, the Elephant House, the Palm House and the artificial rock formations. The renovation also created Hungary's first public aquarium. The Palm House is now called America Tropicana and presents the flora and fauna of the tropical Americas.

The zoo was badly hit in the Second World War. Air raids from autumn 1944 damaged it, as it lay near a railway marshalling yard, and the worst destruction came in the Siege of Budapest. According to the zoo's account, only about two dozen of roughly 2,500 animals survived the winter and most buildings were in ruins; Wikipedia gives a lower figure for the survivors, so the exact number should be treated as approximate. It reopened on 1 May 1945 with fewer than a hundred animals, and the park was even ploughed to grow fodder.

Repairs and modernisation continued after the war. A comprehensive reconstruction began in the mid-1990s, restoring the monument-protected animal houses and bringing enclosures up to modern welfare standards. In 2014 land from the closed neighbouring amusement park was returned to the zoo. The result is a zoo where the historic Art Nouveau buildings still stand beside modern enclosures.
Good to know
Look at the main gate and the Elephant House as architecture as well as animal houses; they date from the 1909-1912 reconstruction.
Check the zoo's official website for current opening times, tickets and which houses are open.
The zoo is inside City Park, so it combines easily with other City Park sights.

historyIntro: Budapest Zoo brings together animal care, botanical collections and historic architecture in a City Park institution more than 150 years old.

children.text: Established in the nineteenth century, the zoo formed part of Budapest's growing interest in nature, education and leisure. Its location in City Park placed animal collections among the city's other developing public attractions.

The zoo is known not only for animals but for decorative architecture and planted spaces. Its role has changed with modern approaches to animal welfare, conservation and education; today's exhibits should be judged by current information, not historic conditions.

stories.title: Scientists and film stars among the visitors

children.text: The zoo's own history page says it has welcomed many renowned biologists, from Nobel laureate Konrad Lorenz to Joy Adamson, as well as several international film stars, among them Richard Burton.

name: Hospital in the Rock
description: A wartime emergency hospital built in the cave system under Castle Hill, later a secret Cold War nuclear bunker and now a museum. It treated casualties in the 1944 to 1945 siege and the 1956 uprising, and its wards and equipment can be seen on a guided tour.

children.text: The Hospital in the Rock and Nuclear Bunker Museum is housed in a natural cave system under Castle Hill, about ten kilometres long according to the museum's history page, which Budapest residents have used since the Middle Ages. The museum is at Lovas út 4/c and is run by a public benefit foundation. The first room built in the caves was the Air Raid Alarm Control Centre, which controlled the sirens in the Castle district from 1937 to 1945.

The hospital itself was built between 1941 and 1943 using existing cave tunnels, with caverns becoming wards and passages becoming corridors. It was ordered by Károly Szendy, then Budapest mayor and minister of war, and operated under St. John's Hospital. It opened on 20 February 1944 with three wards and one operating theatre. During the siege of 1944 and 1945 all 94 beds were constantly occupied and patients also lay in the cave corridors. The hospital had its own generators and could take X-rays when hospitals on the surface could not.

The history page records that eight Jewish doctors were assigned there to labour service, that Dr. Kálmán Koppány helped prevent their deportation, and that two of them were betrayed in November 1944 and one was killed. The breakout from the Castle came on 11 February 1945, after which less serious patients left and the rest were transferred. The museum's history page gives July 1945 as the closing date, while another account says June 1945. Other accounts give very different figures for how many wounded were treated at the peak of the siege.

In the 1950s the hospital became a top-secret institution with the code LOSK 0101/1, declassified in 2002. When the 1956 revolution began it reopened to treat civilians and soldiers, with Dr. András Máthé as head surgeon, and it operated until December 1956. Between 1958 and 1962 it was converted into a nuclear bunker with a ventilation system with a gas filter, a water supply connected to the Danube and two Ganz diesel engines. The plan was for medical staff to enter first and open the hospital for other survivors after 72 hours.

A caretaker family looked after the site until 2004, and the Krétakör Theatre Company staged performances there from 2004 to 2006. Renovation began in 2007, and it has been continuously open as an exhibition since 11 March 2008. Wikipedia notes that it features waxwork recreations of treatments and siege-era scenes.
Good to know
Visits are by guided tour; check the official Hospital in the Rock site for current tours, languages, tickets and booking.
A visitor guide suggests the Buda Castle Funicular from Clark Ádám Square, or bus lines 16, 16A or 116 to Dísz tér; check current routes before travelling.
The museum is a short walk from Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.
Guest reviews on the museum's site describe the tour as moving; it presents wartime suffering and the 1956 uprising.

historyIntro: Deep beneath Buda Castle, a former emergency hospital traces Budapest's wartime siege, the 1956 Revolution and the anxious decades of the Cold War. The underground rooms tell a very human story of medicine, improvisation and survival.

historySections.heading: A hospital built into the Castle Hill caves

children.text: The natural limestone cave network beneath Buda Castle was adapted to shelter residents during air raids. Construction of an underground emergency hospital began in 1941, and it opened on 20 February 1944. Its facilities included three wards and an operating theatre.

During the siege of Budapest in 1944–45, its beds and connecting passages filled with wounded civilians and soldiers. Medical staff worked amid shortages and difficult conditions, while the subterranean location helped protect the hospital from bombing above.

The hospital reopened during the Hungarian Revolution of October 1956. Its doctors treated wounded people from both civilian and military backgrounds, and the space also sheltered families. The facility continued treating patients until December of that year.

historySections.heading: From hospital to nuclear bunker and museum

children.text: Between 1958 and 1962, the complex was adapted for a possible nuclear or chemical emergency. New ventilation, filtration and backup power systems reflected the anxieties of the Cold War. The facility remained a controlled civil-defence site for decades.

The underground complex was eventually opened to the public as a museum, with permanent exhibition operations from 2008. Today it offers an unusual way to understand twentieth-century Budapest through the stories of patients, volunteers and medical staff.

stories.title: The surgeon who wore a recovered bullet

children.text: The museum's historical account describes Dr András Máthé, who worked here during the 1956 Revolution. According to the museum, he wore a bullet on a necklace that he had removed from an injured patient's head. It is a striking account of the dangerous surgeries performed underground.
This is presented as an account recorded by the museum, not as a supernatural legend.

stories.sourceLabel: Hospital in the Rock — historical accounts

stories.title: A persistent myth about Soviet flamethrowers

children.text: The museum specifically disputes a story that Soviet troops burned out the Hospital in the Rock with flamethrowers in 1945. Its official history says this confusion relates to fighting elsewhere in the wider cave system, not the hospital wards.
A responsible guide should distinguish this documented correction from the dramatic version of the story.
